fields.Text: Coupling patterns from worst to best: {{c1::Concrete + Instantiate}}, {{c2::Concrete + Inject}}, {{c3::Abstract + Instantiate}}, {{c4::Abstract + Inject}} (DIP).

fields.Back: The class creates and owns a concrete type itself; tightest coupling, least flexible. Checkout has Paypal processor; as an owned member.
The class receives a concrete type from outside (e.g., Checkout(Paypal& p)); avoids creation but is still tied to the concretion.
The class depends on an abstraction (IPaymentProcessor exists) but still instantiates concretes inside (Paypal p1; Stripe p2;); gains polymorphism, still rigid.
The class depends only on the abstraction (IPaymentProcessor& processor) and concretes are injected at runtime; Dependency Inversion Principle; most flexible and testable.

fields.Front: Which UML relationship corresponds to 'instantiate' patterns, and which to 'inject' patterns?
fields.Back: Instantiate = Composition (class owns what it creates); Inject = Aggregation (class holds a reference to something created elsewhere).

fields.Front: In C++, how is composition typically expressed versus aggregation in the slides?
fields.Back: Composition: member held by value (Paypal processor;). Aggregation: member held by reference (Paypal& processor; or IPaymentProcessor& processor;) bound in the constructor.

fields.Front: What is the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) as illustrated by Checkout?
fields.Back: High-level Checkout depends only on the abstraction IPaymentProcessor, not on concrete Paypal/Stripe; concretes are injected.

fields.Front: Write the IPaymentProcessor interface from the slides.
fields.Back: class IPaymentProcessor { public: virtual ~IPaymentProcessor() = default; virtual void pay(double amount) = 0; };

fields.Front: Why does an interface need virtual ~IPaymentProcessor() = default;?
fields.Back: A virtual destructor ensures the derived class destructor runs when deleting through a base-class pointer.
Constructor injection: the member reference processor is bound to whatever concrete processor is passed in.

fields.Text: In pattern 4 (Abstract + Inject), Checkout c1(paypal); c1.process(120.0); prints `{{c1::Paid $120 with Paypal}} and Checkout c2(stripe); c2.process(80.0); prints {{c2::Paid $80 with Stripe}}`.

fields.Front: Why is processor.pay(amount) in pattern 4 called a polymorphic call?
fields.Back: pay is virtual and processor is a reference to the base type, so the actual object's override (Paypal::pay or Stripe::pay) is chosen at runtime.

fields.Front: What is the guiding principle of the coupling-choices lecture?

fields.Text: Coupling pattern summary: Concrete + Instantiate = Checkout creates a Paypal itself → {{c1::Composition}}; Concrete + Inject = Checkout receives a Paypal → {{c2::Aggregation}}.
Coupling pattern summary: Abstract + Instantiate = depends on IPaymentProcessor but still news concretes → {{c1::Composition}}; Abstract + Inject = gets concretes injected → {{c2::Aggregation}}.
The most flexible and testable dependency pattern is {{c1::Abstract + Inject}}, which implements the {{c2::Dependency Inversion Principle}}.
A C++ interface is a class containing only {{c1::pure virtual}} functions (declared with {{c2::`= 0`}}) plus a virtual destructor.
